purpose: Adalimumab-bwwd is used to treat conditions where your immune system is overactive and causing inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and plaque psoriasis. It helps reduce pain, swelling, and other symptoms so you can feel better and do more of your daily activities. It is a biosimilar, meaning it works just like the original brand-name medication Humira.
how_it_works: Your body makes a protein called TNF (tumor necrosis factor) that can cause too much inflammation when your immune system is out of balance. Adalimumab-bwwd attaches to that TNF protein and blocks it, which helps calm down the inflammation. Think of it like a key that fits into a lock — it plugs up the TNF so it can't cause as much damage to your joints, skin, or digestive system.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are redness, itching, or pain at the injection site where you give yourself the shot. You may also notice headaches, a runny nose, or rash. Some people get stomach pain or nausea. These are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Because this medication lowers your immune system's activity, you have a higher chance of getting serious infections, including tuberculosis (TB) — your doctor will test you for TB before you start. Tell your doctor right away if you develop a fever, chills, cough, or flu-like symptoms. It may also increase the risk of certain cancers, like lymphoma. Avoid live vaccines while taking this medication. Do not use it if you have an active infection. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on what condition is being treated. For many adults with rheumatoid arthritis or similar conditions, the typical dose is 40 mg injected under the skin every other week. Some conditions may require a higher starting dose or more frequent injections. It comes as a prefilled pen or syringe that you inject at home. Your doctor or nurse will show you exactly how to use it.
